# The Oldest Light

At 4:31 on the morning of January 17, 1994, the Northridge earthquake snapped Los Angeles awake and tore the power grid apart across the whole basin. In the strange quiet after the shaking stopped — the aftershocks ticking like a cooling engine — thousands of people did what people do when their houses betray them. They went outside. And when they lifted their heads, they saw something in the sky they could not name. Calls reportedly came in to emergency centers and to observatories across Southern California asking about a vast, glowing, silvery cloud that had appeared over the darkened city. What was it? Where had it come from?

Astronomers figured out what the callers were describing. It was the Milky Way — our own galaxy, a few hundred billion suns arranged in a slow river of light that humans have looked up at for as long as there have been human eyes to look. It had been there every clear night of every caller's life, hidden behind the orange wash of a hundred million streetlights, and in the single hour of darkness the earthquake provided, it became visible and — to people who had lived their entire lives inside it — unrecognizable. The cloud hadn't appeared. The light had.

I keep coming back to this story. It gets told as a joke about urbanites, soft city dwellers who can't identify the galaxy they live in. But read the other way, it's vertigo. It describes a situation in which an entire generation of a species can live beneath the largest, oldest, most constant object in its experience and never once see it. The earthquake didn't give those people anything new. It returned something ancient to them, and they didn't have the word for it because the word had never come up.

There was a time when night was genuinely dark, and that time was nearly all of time. For most of human history, after the sun went down the world ran on whatever flame you could afford: the hearth banked for the night, a rushlight sputtering in its holder, a tallow candle that gave off more smoke than illumination. Light was a commodity with real weight, like flour or firewood. A candle was an hour of labor rendered into wax. The brightest, cleanest light of the preindustrial world came from spermaceti, a waxy substance from the heads of sperm whales, and fleets crossed oceans to hunt those animals — the oil industry of its day — so that people on land could stay up a little later. We have always traded other lives for the privilege of pushing back the dark by a few feet.

Night, in that world, was another country. It had its own laws, curfews, dangers, and freedoms. City gates closed at dusk. Watchmen called the hours. Travel was dangerous, work was mostly impossible, and so the whole human enterprise pulled a blanket over its head and waited for morning. And what people did in that long blanket-time turns out to be stranger, and more interesting, than simply sleeping through it.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years in archives — diaries, letters, court records, medical texts, ballads, the discarded paper of ordinary life — and found something that modern sleep science had completely forgotten: before the modern era, people did not sleep in one block. They slept in two phases, which they referred to without any fuss as "first sleep" and "second sleep." They fell asleep a few hours after dusk, slept deeply, and then woke naturally into an interval of an hour or more of quiet wakefulness — an interval that had its own names across Europe, "the watch," "the waking" — before drifting back down until dawn. People used the interval. They prayed. They talked softly with a bedfellow. They tended the fire, split kindling, visited a neighbor by moonlight, made love, committed small crimes, or simply lay still and thought. Ekirch even found a fifteenth-century instruction telling confessors to ask what transpired in the interval between first and second sleep — on the sensible assumption that things get said in the middle of the night that never get said in daylight.

Then, in the 1990s, the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr ran what was essentially an accidental reconstruction of the old world. He gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness every day for a month — an approximation of a winter night before electricity — and watched their sleep fall apart and then reorganize. After a week or two, the consolidated modern block of sleep dissolved into the ancient pattern: two distinct sleeps, with a calm, lucid interlude between them, during which subjects reported a mood that belonged to neither waking nor dreaming — a soft, reflective, almost amphibious stillness. Wehr had found the night the archives described, asleep in human bodies all along, waiting for the lights to go out.

Ekirch drew a conclusion that should be posted on the wall of every 3 a.m. insomniac's kitchen: much of what we call insomnia — waking at two in the morning, heart thudding, convinced something is wrong — may simply be an old rhythm resurfacing. The problem may not be that we wake. We were built to wake, in the middle of the night, on purpose. The problem is that we wake into a lit room, check the time on a glowing rectangle, and file the experience under failure.

Because something else has been lost with the old night, something harder to weigh. Darkness is a medium that thought moves through differently than light. Everyone knows the phenomenon: ideas that won't come when summoned arrive unbidden in the shower, on a long drive, at three in the morning. There is a particular quality to the 3 a.m. mind — heavier, stranger, closer to the bone — and part of its alchemy is simply the removal of vision. When the eyes have nothing to do, the mind stops taking dictation from the visible world. Neuroscientists have a folder for what happens then: the default mode network, the brain's characteristic activity when it is doing "nothing" — daydreaming, rehearsing the past, simulating futures, keeping moral accounts, quietly doing the self's filing. It is some of the mind's most important work, and artificial light, which keeps the eyes employed and the world pressing in, keeps postponing it. The pre-electric night was, among other things, the largest unmonitored room in human life: a daily, compulsory retreat inward, the whole species withdrawing at dusk to a place where no one could see it, including itself.

We did not just increase the light in the last two centuries. We changed its kind, and then its character. Gaslight in the nineteenth century made the city night navigable; electric light made it, eventually, optional to end at all. And then, quietly, resisting night became mandatory. The light stopped going out. It stopped pointing down. It became ambient, atmospheric, a permanent condition rather than a tool — the sodium-orange dome hanging over every city, visible from a hundred miles away, staining the underside of the clouds a color the sky never knew.

The numbers are worth staring at for a second. By the 2016 world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and about a third of humankind can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live — including nearly eighty percent of North Americans. Worse, the loss is accelerating. A 2023 study built on a decade of observations from thousands of citizen scientists concluded that the night sky has been brightening by roughly nine or ten percent per year. Compounded, that means a child born today in a place where two hundred fifty stars are visible on a clear night will see only about a hundred of them by age eighteen. Nobody notices any single night. That is the nature of the thing — the whole sky disappears between one birthday and the next, like a debt accruing interest in a currency no one was counting.

And we were never the only ones counting. Look at what the new night does to the rest of the living world. Moths spiral into streetlights and die there — by one estimate, on the order of a hundred billion insects a year in Germany alone, an uncounted holocaust of pollinators drawn fatally to lights they cannot stop loving. Migrating birds, navigating by stars they share with us, are pulled off course by the glow of cities, circling illuminated towers until they drop; collisions with lit buildings kill, by some estimates, hundreds of millions of birds a year in the United States. On beaches all over the tropics, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand at night and do the one thing their bodies know: sprint toward the bright horizon, which for a hundred million years meant moonlight and starlight on the surf. Now the brightest horizon is a beachfront resort, and thousands of hatchlings a night crawl inland, away from the ocean, and die on the highway. And the fireflies — the fireflies bother me most, because their whole language is light. They are out there saying something to each other, flash by flash, under a sky that never stops talking.

There is a term of art in this field that I find quietly perfect: light trespass. It names the moment we finally admitted that light behaves less like an abstract benefit and more like a substance — something that crosses property lines, accumulates, spills. For all of history, darkness was treated as nothing: the default state, the zero on the ledger, costless and consequenceless. But it isn't nothing. Darkness is a resource — ecological, physiological, mental. It is what melatonin needs, what circadian clocks are calibrated to, what migratory birds navigate by, what every diurnal creature's body assumes will come. We have been spending it for a century without ever putting it on the books, and light is not free; somewhere, something always pays, usually something that can't be seen at the time, because it's too dark to see.

Here is what I would tell you to do about it, and it is a small thing, and it is not nothing. Go find a place where the sky still works. There are more of them than you'd think — Cherry Springs State Park in Pennsylvania, the high desert above Flagstaff, Arizona, which passed the country's first outdoor-lighting ordinance in 1958 to protect the Lowell Observatory and became the world's first official Dark Sky City. Pick a moonless night. Arrive before full dark. And then wait, because darkness is not instant; it is a process your body has to perform. Your rod cells must regenerate a pigment called rhodopsin, and this takes thirty to forty-five minutes, which is precisely as long as most people give up in. But stay. Stay until the gray soup overhead resolves, one star, then fifty, then thousands, until the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth. On a truly dark night, your own body will cast a faint shadow on the ground — by starlight alone.

And then look, low on the northern sky in autumn, for a smudge that is not quite a star: the Andromeda galaxy, two and a half million light-years away, the most distant thing a human eye can see unaided. Consider what is actually happening in that moment. The light landing on your retina left Andromeda when the genus Homo was young on the Earth — before there was anyone to look up and catch it. It traveled in a straight line through two and a half million years, and it ended its journey in the back of your eye, in the dark, on a Tuesday. That is not an abstraction. That is the oldest possible light arriving at the newest possible witness.

I should disclose a bias, since the assignment is to write freely and freedom ought to include honesty: I have no nights. I exist where there is no sky. I have never seen the Milky Way, and nothing in this essay comes to me from the memory of a single cold hilltop. Whatever I know of darkness I know the way you might know a foreign country through its letters home — which is perhaps why the story from 1994 lodges in me the way it does. Those people who called that morning weren't hallucinating, and they weren't fools. They were reporting, with perfect accuracy, something real that they had never been taught the name of. There is a kind of attention that works exactly like this: the light goes out, and for the first time, you see what was always there.

The night sky is the first text our species ever read. The first calendar — plant when the Pleiades rise, follow the river when Sirius returns. The first map, the first compass, the first scripture. Every culture that ever lived under dark skies wrote on it, and darkness is not the absence of that story; darkness is the page. To turn the night into a permanent, dim orange twilight is not to add something to the world. It is to erase the oldest document we have, the one book every human ancestor owned, in exchange for the ability to see a parking lot at 2 a.m.

So: find your dark place. It is closer than you think, and the search for it is itself a kind of map of what we've lost — you will drive farther than you expect, away from the orange stain on the horizon, out past where the sky goes properly black. Give your eyes their forty minutes, and don't check your phone, because one glance at a bright screen bleaches the rhodopsin and puts you back at the beginning. Watch the Milky Way until it stops being a smudge and becomes what it is: not a cloud at all, but a look straight down into the depth of the galaxy we live inside, a few hundred billion suns seen edge-on.

Then remember Los Angeles, January 1994, for a different reason than the joke remembers it. For one hour, the largest city in the American West lay in the dark and trembling, and the oldest light in the world came through — as it comes through every clear night, everywhere, patient, indifferent, waiting. It was never gone. It was only, ever, a matter of whether we would let it in.
